name: Olga Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's all right. My mother said I shouldn't talk to strangers about money, so I may keep a few things back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's completely fine. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner in an underground potash mine, a kilometre down. A continuous miner is a long machine with a spinning cutting head that chews through the salt rock and loads it onto a conveyor, no blasting. I lead a crew of four on day shift, and I've been the top cutter on our panel for two years. My grandfather worked this same mine, and my father still does, on maintenance. I like the quiet down there between cuts and the fact that everybody knows their place. What tires me out is the new managers from head office who change the rules every six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we can get back to work. People in the city get excited about every new gadget, and then it turns out a person still has to do the job. I wouldn't put anything online, I'm not on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, and I'm glad of it. I'd have the life I planned: the mine, the wedding, a house near my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing now. Keep cutting, keep saving, get married next summer and put a deposit on the old Schmidt house on Mill Lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My younger brother uses them for school, and I don't like it. If a boy can't write his own essay, what's he going to do when the roof talks to him underground? You have to listen with your own ears down there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's on the calendar for you this coming year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding in June at St Anne's, with Piotr. He works at the feed mill. Then the house, if the Schmidts will sell to us.

S0.say: She'd say good, everyone can get back to work, because city people get excited by every gadget until it turns out a person still has to do the job. She isn't online, so she wouldn't post.
S0.think: She's glad nothing changes, because it leaves the life she planned intact: the mine, the wedding and a house near her parents.
S0.do: Keeps cutting and saving, marries Piotr next June at St Anne's, and puts a deposit on the old Schmidt house on Mill Lane.
S0.quote: If a boy can't write his own essay, what's he going to do when the roof talks to him underground?
S0.fieldNote: Olga's world is rooted in family, church and the mine her grandfather worked. She distrusts AI on principle and worries about what it does to young people's skills, using her brother as an example. Her plans are traditional and close to home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some of it is fine, but don't take away the jobs that hold a town together. A mine isn't just a business, it's where families eat from. I'd say that at work and at church coffee after the service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be worried for the young men on my crew more than for myself. I'm good, they'd keep me as long as they can. But I've seen what happened when the salt plant automated, half the families on our street had to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep my head down. I wouldn't go on any computer course unless they made me. I'd save more, maybe hold off on the bigger house and buy the smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't like it, but I could live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Continuous miners can already be run from a distance in some mines. Has that come up at yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head office talked about it last year, a remote cabin on the surface. Nobody who's never smelled a kilometre of salt should be driving my machine from a chair upstairs. My father said wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you go if your mine changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are two other potash mines within an hour, and they'd take me. But I wouldn't want to leave. I'd rather stay and fight it out at this one.

S1.say: She'd say some automation is fine, but not if it takes away the jobs that hold a town together, because a mine is where families eat from. She'd say it at work and at church coffee.
S1.think: She worries more for the young men on her crew than herself, having seen half her street move away when the salt plant automated.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and only takes computer training if required. Saves more and considers buying the smaller house instead of the bigger one.
S1.feel: Uneasy, disliking it but able to live with it.
S1.quote: Nobody who's never smelled a kilometre of salt should be driving my machine from a chair upstairs.
S1.fieldNote: Olga sees the mine as a community institution, not just a business. Her memory of the salt plant automating gives her worry a concrete shape. She has options nearby but wants to stay put out of loyalty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody asks ordinary people. A few men in California decide, and the rest of us pay. I'd say it loud for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the end of what my family has done for three generations. My grandfather dug this mine with a pick, and I'll be the one who hands it to a machine. That's what it means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house plans and keep every penny in the bank. I'd talk to my parents about the old farm my grandmother left us, because land is the one thing that holds. I'd lean on church and family, and cut back on everything that isn't needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still marry, but smaller. A meal in the church hall, not the hotel. My mother would cry about it more than I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents and Father Tomasz. And Piotr's family, they're good people. I wouldn't go to the government for help unless it was the last thing left.

S2.say: She'd say this is what happens when nobody asks ordinary people: a few men in California decide and everyone else pays. She'd say it loudly for once.
S2.think: She sees it as the end of three generations of her family working the mine, with her as the one who hands it to a machine.
S2.do: Stops the house plans, keeps her savings in the bank and cuts back on everything non-essential. Talks with her parents about her grandmother's old farm, holds a smaller wedding in the church hall, and leans on family and church.
S2.quote: My grandfather dug this mine with a pick, and I'll be the one who hands it to a machine.
S2.fieldNote: Olga's alarm is about lineage and identity as much as income. She blames distant tech elites rather than the mine. She turns to family, church and land, and would only seek government help as a last resort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's not wreck towns in a rush. I'd want limits on how fast mines can let people go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still the end of mining for me, just later. I'd be thirty-two with a husband, maybe a child, and no work. That scares me more than two years, in a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cutting and saving, and get married as planned. I'd pay off the smaller house before anything else. In the second year I'd start working the farm with Piotr on weekends, getting the fences and the barn back in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but always thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the old farm. Is that a real option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. It's twenty hectares and the soil's decent, but nobody's farmed it for ten years. I'd rather be poor on my own land than paid to do nothing in a town with no mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you vote or speak up in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote for whoever promised to keep mines open with people in them. I might write a letter to the paper. I wouldn't march, that's not me.

S3.say: She'd say there are five years, so towns shouldn't be wrecked in a rush, and she'd want limits on how fast mines can let people go.
S3.think: She thinks it's still the end of mining for her, landing at 32 with a husband, maybe a child and no work, which scares her in a different way.
S3.do: Keeps cutting and saving, marries as planned and pays off the smaller house first. From the second year, works her family's farm with Piotr on weekends and votes for candidates who'd keep people in mines.
S3.feel: Anxious, thinking about it constantly without panicking.
S3.quote: I'd rather be poor on my own land than paid to do nothing in a town with no mine.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Olga's thoughts turn to her grandmother's twenty-hectare farm as a place to live independently. She prefers being poor on her own land to receiving support. Her politics are quiet: voting and perhaps a letter, not marching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change. Maybe it won't happen at all. People should stay calm and keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get most of my working life at the mine, which is what I wanted. Ten years is time to marry, have children, get the farm going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as planned for now. Marry, buy the house, keep cutting. Around year five I'd start getting the farm ready properly, maybe some sheep and a vegetable patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, but far enough away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years puts you at thirty-seven. What would you want by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two or three children, the house paid off, and the farm working. If a machine is digging my potash in 2036, I want my children feeding chickens, not watching screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there something you'd do now that you wouldn't do otherwise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach my brother how to fix things with his hands. Fences, engines, the old way. He'll need it more than I will.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a long time and it may not happen at all, so people should stay calm and keep working.
S4.think: She thinks she'd get most of her working life at the mine as planned, with time to marry, have children and get the farm going.
S4.do: Carries on with the wedding, house and mine for now, and starts preparing the family farm around year five with sheep and a vegetable patch. Teaches her younger brother hands-on repair skills.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but it feels far enough away.
S4.quote: If a machine is digging my potash in 2036, I want my children feeding chickens, not watching screens.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Olga keep her traditional plan almost intact and put the farm in place as a fallback. Her focus is on her future children's way of life. She'd pass on practical skills to her brother rather than any new technology.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time to get the farm ready or to have the wedding properly. What would help is rules that make companies keep people on longer, and help for young families to stay on the land.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A machine doesn't pray before it goes down, and I think that matters, even if I can't tell you why. That's all.

headlineQuote: A machine doesn't pray before it goes down, and I think that matters, even if I can't tell you why.
portrait: Olga Weber is 27, the top continuous miner operator and day-shift crew lead at an underground potash mine where her grandfather and father worked before her. She is engaged to Piotr, who works at a feed mill, plans a June wedding at St Anne's, never uses AI and leans on church and family. She is calm and content if AI fizzles, uneasy in Steady Disruption, and alarmed when AGI comes in two years and threatens three generations of mining. With five or ten years, her plan turns to her grandmother's twenty-hectare farm, a paid-off house and raising children on the land.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there would be no time to get the farm ready or have the wedding properly.
whatWouldHelp: Rules making companies keep people on longer, and help for young families to stay on the land.
